title: The One With The Candy Hearts

jokes.text: The Rachel thing's not happening, your ex-wife's a lesbian, you...
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to convince Ross to get back in the dating game.
jokes.punchline: Joey's pep talk lists Ross's romantic failures so bluntly — including the lesbian ex-wife — that it becomes a brutal comedy of stacking misfortune.
jokes.explanation: Works as casual cruelty from Joey — he means well but his catalogue of Ross's failures is darkly funny. The incomplete trailing sentence implies there's more but it's too much to list.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I barely know her. We've had minimal contact.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Minimal contact? She borrowed an egg from you?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: If a woman borrows an egg, you're in! That's like, a step away from her asking you to father her children!

jokes.text: Excuse me. Could we get an egg over here, still in the shell?
jokes.setup: Ross says the woman only knows him because she lent him an egg once. Joey and Chandler are scheming how he can approach her.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's solution is to literally order an egg from the restaurant so Ross can return it — an absurdly overcomplicated social strategy.
jokes.explanation: The joke works because it takes a simple social situation and applies manic, literal logic to it. Very Chandler in its over-engineered absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hey! What's up? I was just, uh... in the neighborhood. Totally casual. Not like I planned this or anything. I mean, I did, but like, in a cool way.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So anyway, how have you been? You look great. I mean, you always look great. Not that I notice. I mean, I notice, but like, everyone notices. I'm just... saying words now, aren't I?

jokes.text: Go up to her and say, 'Here's your egg back. I'm returning your egg.'
jokes.setup: The egg scheme is being pitched to Ross.
jokes.punchline: Chandler delivers the proposed script with complete sincerity — the joke is that this insane plan is being sold as perfectly reasonable romantic advice.
jokes.explanation: Escalates the absurdity of joke #1 by having Chandler actually script out the dialogue. The deadpan delivery of a profoundly stupid plan is classic Chandler.

jokes.text: It's suicide. The man's got an egg.
jokes.setup: Ross has taken the egg and is approaching the woman. Joey is optimistic.
jokes.punchline: Chandler undercuts Joey's enthusiasm with a perfectly deadpan death sentence: the visual of a grown man holding an egg as a romantic gambit is all you need.
jokes.explanation: This is the payoff of the egg bit and it's excellent. Maximum economy — six words capture the entire absurdity of the situation. 'The man's got an egg' is quintessentially quotable and perfectly Chandler. The construction is tight: dismiss, pause, explain. Earns its high score.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: We go in there, we act like we own the place. Confidence is key.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, we're returning eggs. We didn't buy eggs. We're going to get arrested.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I've done this a hundred times. They never check.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You've returned eggs a hundred times?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, not eggs specifically. But the principle is the same.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The principle of committing fraud?

jokes.text: She's only going out with me because I'm bringing a friend for her friend.
jokes.setup: Chandler is reluctant to go on the double date. Joey reveals the condition of his own date.
jokes.punchline: Joey admits his date is entirely transactional — she's using him as a vehicle for her friend's date — and he says this without any apparent embarrassment.
jokes.explanation: Mild self-deprecating joke from Joey that reveals character — he has no dignity about being used as a matchmaking pawn and doesn't care. Functional but not sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So what are Ross's chances with this whole egg thing?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I'd say they're about as good as my chances of becoming a astronaut, which is to say, slim to none. And Slim just left town.

jokes.text: Pathetic mess. I know, but... Come on, man, she's needy, she's vulnerable. I'm thinking:
jokes.setup: Joey is pitching why Chandler should come on the date by describing the friend he'll be paired with.
jokes.punchline: Joey's selling point for the date is that the woman is 'needy and vulnerable' — framed as an opportunity, with an unspoken punchline about what Joey thinks that means for Chandler's chances.
jokes.explanation: The dark implication that vulnerability is Joey's sales pitch makes this funny — it's a window into Joey's unsophisticated but cheerfully amoral worldview.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I date creeps all the time!

jokes.text: Still got the egg, huh?
jokes.setup: Ross returns from his approach to the woman, egg still in hand, apparently having succeeded.
jokes.punchline: Joey's only observation is that the egg is still there — the callback lands because we know the egg was the absurd centerpiece of the scheme.
jokes.explanation: Final button on the egg arc. Economical callback that rewards the audience for tracking the bit. Works because it's understated — Joey says everything by saying almost nothing.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: She was pathetic and needy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So you're saying there's a chance?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No! I see vulnerability as an opportunity.

jokes.text: How do I look? Oh, um... ...I don't care.
jokes.setup: Chandler asks Joey how he looks before the date — a vulnerable moment.
jokes.punchline: Joey's answer is a theatrical pause followed by complete indifference. The 'um' makes it funnier — it implies he considered it and still couldn't muster caring.
jokes.explanation: The pause-then-dismissal structure is perfectly executed. The '...I don't care' is so flat it becomes its own punchline. Classic bromance indifference humor, well constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So how do I look?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Like you're about to go on a date and make some poor woman very happy... for about twenty minutes.

jokes.text: And what did you bring? She's checking her coat.
jokes.setup: Lorraine praises Joey's date (Chandler) then asks what Joey 'brought' — implying his date.
jokes.punchline: Joey's date has not yet arrived; the woman checking her coat is the implication that his offering is delayed or perhaps disappointing.
jokes.explanation: Sets up the Janice reveal efficiently but isn't especially funny on its own — it's structural comedy, preparing the bigger joke to come.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh. My. God.

jokes.text: Chandler's slow-motion horror reaction upon seeing Janice — 'Oh... ...my... ...God.'
jokes.setup: Joey has set Chandler up on a blind date. Chandler goes to wash his hands. Joey asks for a white zinfandel and 'a glass of red for Janice.' Chandler freezes.
jokes.punchline: The dawning horror of Chandler's realization, stretched across multiple beats, is the joke — the audience sees it coming slightly before Chandler does, making his reaction even funnier.
jokes.explanation: The three-beat 'Oh... my... God' is a masterclass in comedic timing. The deliberate slow-motion pacing of his horror, broken into three separate beats, builds anticipation and lands hard. It's also perfectly character-specific — Chandler's reaction to Janice is always theatrical. The studio audience would erupt here.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can't go out with Janice! I'd rather jump out the window!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, we're on the second floor.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'll take my chances!

jokes.text: Okay, I'm making a break for it. I'm going out the window.
jokes.setup: Chandler has just seen that his blind date is Janice — his recently dumped ex.
jokes.punchline: His immediate instinct is to escape via the window rather than face her — the extremity of the avoidance is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Chandler's flight response is always disproportionate to the situation, which is funny. Jumping out a restaurant window to avoid an ex is a perfect extension of his cowardly-but-lovable character.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more anxious right now? I mean, seriously, my stomach is doing backflips, my palms are sweating, and I can't even... you know... go to the bathroom without having a complete panic attack about whether someone's going to hear me or judge me or—

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh God, I just told you all that, didn't I? This is exactly what I'm talking about!

jokes.text: Can you stop yelling? You're making me nervous... ...and I can't go when I'm nervous.
jokes.setup: Chandler is panicking about Janice. Joey is trying to calm him. They are apparently in the men's restroom.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's request for calm pivots to the deeply mundane and overly personal admission that he can't urinate under stress — a sudden, unexpected TMI that deflates the drama.
jokes.explanation: The bathroomconfession pivot is a great structure — high emotional stakes punctured by a completely mundane bodily function concern. The restraint in how it's delivered (the ellipsis pause) makes it land cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, he was like... *sobbing uncontrollably* 'Oh! Oh! Oh!' *wailing* 'This is so beautiful! You're so beautiful!' *crying hysterically*

jokes.text: Pete the Weeper? Remember the guy that used to cry every time we had sex? 'Oh, was it good for you?'
jokes.setup: The women are commiserating about bad boyfriends. Phoebe mentions Pete Carney.
jokes.punchline: The nickname 'Pete the Weeper' plus the impersonation of a crying man asking 'was it good for you?' — the specificity of the detail makes the joke.
jokes.explanation: The specific, vivid detail of a man crying post-sex and asking 'was it good for you?' is both absurd and uncomfortably believable. The nickname structure (Pete the Weeper) gives it extra punch. Strong joke in the bad-boyfriend catalogue.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know Howard? The guy who always has to win? Everything is a competition with him. I once beat him at Scrabble and he insisted on playing three more games until he won.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It drives me crazy! I can never just have a normal conversation or game with him. He always has to come out on top.

jokes.text: Well, I'd take a little crying any day over Howard, the 'I win' guy. 'I win. I win.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has described Pete the Weeper. Rachel tops it with her own bad boyfriend.
jokes.punchline: 'Howard, the I win guy' — the name itself is the joke, implying he treated sex as a competitive event. The impersonation makes it land.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The concept — a man who treats sex as a competition he 'wins' — is original and specific. The nickname convention (the 'I win guy') echoes Pete the Weeper and creates a comedic structure. The follow-up line 'I went out with him for two months. I didn't get to win once' adds a second punchline that's equally sharp. Highly quotable and genuinely original.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, maybe we're attracted to them because on some level we believe we don't deserve to be happy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Or maybe it's because we're all like digital watches... we light up and we beep, and nobody knows why.

jokes.text: I went out with him for two months. I didn't get to win once.
jokes.setup: Rachel has described Howard the 'I win' guy and his post-sex declaration.
jokes.punchline: The complaint isn't that the behavior was disturbing — it's that she never got to win. Accepting the insane premise and playing it straight is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The second punchline of the Howard bit and arguably funnier than the first. By complaining that she 'didn't get to win once,' Rachel completely accepts the absurd competitive framework of sex — which is funnier than rejecting it. Perfect economy, sharp construction, and completely unexpected angle. This is the episode's strongest individual line.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You should follow the advice my bald friend gave me.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Why would I take advice from someone who made the choice to be bald?

jokes.text: I think we're like some kind of magnets. I know I am. That's why I can't wear a digital watch.
jokes.setup: The women are asking why they attract terrible men. Monica says they must be magnets.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe takes the metaphor literally — she believes she is literally magnetic, which is why she can't wear a digital watch. The non-sequitur scientific explanation is pure Phoebe.
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Phoebe. Only she would hear 'we're like magnets' and interpret it literally, then provide a pseudo-scientific explanation (can't wear a digital watch) delivered with total sincerity. The joke is entirely dependent on character — it couldn't come from anyone else. The specificity of 'digital watch' as evidence of her literal magnetism is the detail that elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You could bury them in the ground and let the Earth swallow your sorrow.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Or you could dance around them naked with sticks.

jokes.text: Pheebs, this woman is voluntarily bald.
jokes.setup: Phoebe says her friend Abby, who shaves her head, recommends a cleansing ritual.
jokes.punchline: Monica's skepticism is expressed entirely through the single qualifier 'voluntarily bald' — implying this disqualifies Abby as a credible source.
jokes.explanation: Economical and sharp. Three words ('voluntarily bald') carry all the judgment Monica needs to express. The word 'voluntarily' does a lot of work — it distinguishes chosen baldness from medical baldness and maximizes the absurdity.

jokes.text: It's Valentine's Day. It's perfect. Okay, well, what kind of ritual? We can burn the stuff they gave us. Or we can chant and dance around naked, you know, with sticks.
jokes.setup: Phoebe proposes a cleansing ritual from her friend Abby (who voluntarily shaves her head) to break the bad-boyfriend cycle.
jokes.punchline: The alternative to burning things — naked chanting with sticks — is presented as a completely reasonable option. Monica and Rachel's immediate unified choice of 'burning' is the real punchline.
jokes.explanation: The escalating oddness of Phoebe's options (burning, then naked chanting with sticks) and the instantaneous consensus of the other two to choose burning is well-structured. The sticks detail is the absurdist flourish that makes it.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: I can pick up quarters with my toes.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's impressive, but I have to ask—are you using your plantar fascia or your flexor digitorum brevis?

jokes.text: Burning's good. — Burning's good.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just offered naked stick-dancing as the alternative to burning things in the cleansing ritual.
jokes.punchline: Monica and Rachel simultaneously, flatly choose burning — no deliberation needed. The synchrony implies they didn't even consider the sticks option.
jokes.explanation: The button to Phoebe's naked-sticks joke. Works as a reaction beat — the simultaneous, flat agreement communicates 'we didn't even consider that' without a word of commentary.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: I cut you out of all the photos.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Of course you did.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: But I saved all the heads. Do you want them?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's okay.

jokes.text: You know, ever since I was little, I've been able to pick up quarters with my toes. Yeah? Good for you.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Janice are stuck together after Joey abandons them. The conversation has died.
jokes.punchline: The desperate non-sequitur (toe-quarter dexterity) as a conversation filler, met with Janice's flat 'Good for you' — the joke is the cringe of two people with nothing to say to each other.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'quarters with my toes' as the chosen desperate conversational gambit is perfect. Janice's 'Good for you' with the implied beat before it is the deadpan payoff. Classic awkward date comedy.

jokes.text: Uh, quarters or rolls of quarters?
jokes.setup: Chandler has mentioned picking up quarters with his toes. Janice gives a flat 'Good for you.'
jokes.punchline: Then, after a beat, Janice decides to engage — but her follow-up question is whether it's loose quarters or rolls of quarters, as if the distinction matters. She's either genuinely curious or playing along with the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully constructed two-beat joke. The first beat (Chandler's non-sequitur + Janice's dismissal) sets up a dead end. The second beat subverts it by having Janice actually engage — but with a completely insane follow-up question that treats this as a serious topic. The specificity of 'rolls of quarters' is what elevates it from a decent reaction to a great joke.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I gotta go. I got a date with this girl, and uh, she wants me to help her move some stuff.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, 'move some stuff' is a sexual euphemism.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No it's not!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes it is.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, even if it is, I'm still gonna go help her move stuff. If it's a euphemism, great! If it's not, I'm gonna get a free workout.

jokes.text: By the way, Chandler, I cut you out of all of my pictures. So if you want, I have a bag with just your heads.
jokes.setup: The conversation has found a lull. Janice mentions she cut Chandler out of photos.
jokes.punchline: She has retained the severed heads in a bag and is offering them — the horror-movie implication of 'a bag with just your heads' is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The image of a literal bag of (photo) heads is darkly funny and very specific to Janice's character — the kind of obsessive ex behavior that's played for laughs rather than menace. 'A bag with just your heads' has genuine quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, that's great! You two kids have fun! Don't do anything I wouldn't do. Which, granted, is not a lot, but still!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I hope you have the most wonderful time together. I really do. And I hope you think of me every single second you're apart.

jokes.text: That's okay. Are you sure? Because you could make little puppets out of them. And you could use them in your Theater of Cruelty.
jokes.setup: Chandler declines the bag of his photo-heads.
jokes.punchline: Janice escalates by suggesting he could make puppets from the head-photos and use them in his 'Theater of Cruelty' — a surreally specific and darkly theatrical suggestion.
jokes.explanation: 'Theater of Cruelty' is inspired — it's the kind of specific cultural reference (Artaud's Theatre of Cruelty) that lands as both a real callback and a perfect description of what Janice is proposing. The puppet suggestion preceding it is the setup. Escalation works well here.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Well, at least he has a great sense of humor!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: My fly is down, isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Oh honey, that's just more of you to love!

jokes.text: Tell me it's you and me 'we.' She said she wants to slather my body with stuff and then lick it off. I'm not even sure what slathering is. But I definitely want to be a part of it.
jokes.setup: Joey pulls Chandler aside and says 'we might be leaving now.' Chandler panics, thinking Joey is abandoning him.
jokes.punchline: Joey's reason for leaving is that his date wants to 'slather' him — Joey's confusion about the word 'slathering' paired with his complete enthusiasm regardless of meaning is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey — he doesn't know what slathering means but is 100% on board. The self-awareness about his ignorance combined with zero hesitation captures his character perfectly. Good economy in how quickly this moves.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Don't we have the best friends?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, Joey's more of a long-term investment.

jokes.text: I hope she throws up on you.
jokes.setup: Joey is abandoning Chandler with Janice. Joey apologizes.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's farewell wish is a specific and visceral curse — not 'I hate you' but a precise bodily-fluid outcome he's wishing on Joey.
jokes.explanation: Brief but effective. The specificity of 'throws up on you' (rather than a generic curse) makes it funnier. Perfectly economical — five words, maximum spite.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm gonna spend all of Joey's money.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? Why would you do that?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Because I can. First, I'm buying a yacht.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A yacht?!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Then a private jet. And a mansion in the Hamptons.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Chandler, that's crazy!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, and what exactly is in a mojito? I've always wondered.

jokes.text: I hope she throws up on you.
jokes.setup: Joey is abandoning Chandler alone with Janice on Valentine's Day and leaving his credit card as consolation.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's 'goodbye' to Joey is a cheerful curse — hoping the woman who 'slathers' Joey gets sick on him.
jokes.explanation: Short, sharp, specific. The specificity of 'throw up' rather than a generic insult makes it funnier. Works as a dark button on Joey's betrayal.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Did you know that dogs experience jet lag? It's actually a circadian rhythm disruption. When they travel across time zones, their internal clock becomes desynchronized with the external light-dark cycle, which can cause disorientation, appetite changes, and altered sleep patterns. Fascinating, really.

jokes.text: Although I have enjoyed the fact that your shirt's been sticking out of your zipper since you came back from the bathroom.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Janice have been left alone and agree it's a 'crappy night.' They're making the best of it.
jokes.punchline: Janice reveals she has been watching Chandler walk around with his shirt tucked into his open zipper this whole time and said nothing — a visual embarrassment that we've retroactively imagined.
jokes.explanation: A classic wardrobe malfunction gag elevated slightly by the retroactive revelation — we realize Chandler has been walking around like this during his whole date. The delay of the reveal (she watched and said nothing) is the comedic choice.

dialogue.speaker: Kristen
dialogue.line: So your ex-wife... is she still with her girlfriend?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, they're still together.

dialogue.speaker: Kristen
dialogue.line: That must be weird for you.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You know, it was at first, but I'm really happy for her. She's happy.

jokes.text: How you doing?
jokes.setup: Chandler has gone to fix his zipper situation. He returns and tries to reset the evening.
jokes.punchline: The iconic Joey line 'How you doing?' delivered by Chandler — inappropriate, desperate, and self-aware. It's a meta moment using a catchphrase.
jokes.explanation: Works as a crowd-pleaser because the audience knows this is Joey's line. Chandler using it is a character contrast joke — Joey's effortless charm versus Chandler's awkward attempts at charm. Not deeply crafted but gets a reliable response.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, by the way, Carol's pregnant.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, she and Susan are having a baby.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross! That's huge!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know, I know. Anyway, so I was thinking about getting the new Springsteen album...

jokes.text: Joey's not a friend. He's... a stupid man who left us his credit card.
jokes.setup: Chandler says 'do we have the best friends or what?' in an attempt to reframe the evening positively.
jokes.punchline: Janice corrects him — Joey isn't a friend, he's an asset (a stupid man with a credit card). The pivot from sentimentality to pragmatic exploitation is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Sharp reframe. 'A stupid man who left us his credit card' is a great summary of Joey's utility in this situation. The pause before the reveal ('He's... a stupid man') adds to the delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We need sage branches and sacramental wine for the ritual.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I have some dried oregano from my spice rack and a bottle of Barefoot Cabernet. Will that work?

jokes.text: Another drink? Some dessert? A big-screen TV?
jokes.setup: Chandler and Janice have decided to exploit Joey's credit card. Chandler offers options.
jokes.punchline: The escalation from reasonable restaurant orders (drink, dessert) to absurd retail (big-screen TV) is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Clean escalation joke — the third item breaks the pattern in a satisfying way. The absurdity of ordering a TV at a restaurant is quick and effective.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And I'm gonna need the hair of a man who's never loved a woman.

jokes.text: A bottle of your most overpriced champagne. Each. That's right. Each.
jokes.setup: They've decided to exploit Joey's credit card. Chandler orders champagne.
jokes.punchline: 'Each' — the insistence that they each get their own bottle of the most overpriced champagne is the maximalist punchline. The double 'each' sells it.
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'each' is the comedic device — the confirmation adds swagger to the absurdity. Quick and effective.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I need the semen of a righteous man.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Phoebe, that's not really how it works. I mean, how would you even know if a man was righteous before... you know?

jokes.text: Can you believe this happened? No, no. And yet it did.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Janice have spent Valentine's night together despite him dumping her.
jokes.punchline: 'And yet it did' — the resigned acknowledgment of an improbable situation. The 'no, no' is a shared denial before the concession.
jokes.explanation: Gentle, understated moment of shared absurdity. Works more as a character beat than a full joke — but the resigned humor of 'and yet it did' earns a chuckle.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I have a naked photo of a guy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What? Where did you get that?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He sent it to me.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, let me see!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, but... he's wearing a sweater.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: A sweater? That's not naked!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I know, but it's a really nice sweater.

jokes.text: Goodbye, Janice. Kiss me. Oh, Chandler. Sorry.
jokes.setup: Chandler is saying goodbye to Janice. The implication is they kissed or nearly kissed in the hallway.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's awkward apology ('Oh, Chandler. Sorry') suggests he went in for a kiss and either got rejected or realized mid-attempt he shouldn't be doing this — the physical comedy of a botched goodbye.
jokes.explanation: The physical beat works better on screen than on the page. In transcript form it reads as mild cringe comedy — Chandler's reflexive self-admonishment is the character note.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, it's pure alcohol!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's why you don't leave it on the stove!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Whoa!

jokes.text: Janice is gonna go away now.
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel emerge from the apartment and see Janice in the hallway with Chandler.
jokes.punchline: Chandler speaks about Janice in the third person as if she's an embarrassing problem that can be made to disappear by narrating her departure.
jokes.explanation: The third-person dismissal as a wish-fulfillment tactic is very Chandler — using language to try to control a situation. The flat confidence of 'Janice is gonna go away now' is delightfully absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I mean, what are the odds? In my next life, I'm probably going to come back as a sandwich.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A sandwich that nobody wants to eat.

jokes.text: He just happened to call. Hello, Ross. Yes, that's right. It's me. How did you know?
jokes.setup: Janice is on Chandler's phone in the hallway. Ross approaches.
jokes.punchline: Janice's phone manner — 'Yes, that's right. It's me. How did you know?' — implies the person she's calling knows exactly who she is before she identifies herself, which is both a comment on her notoriety and her theatrical self-presentation.
jokes.explanation: Janice's distinctive personality is so strong that people apparently recognize her voice immediately. The joke is in the self-mythologizing quality of 'how did you know?' — as if her fame precedes her.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Oh, Joey! Come here, you!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, Janice.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: I have something I want to do for you. I promised myself that if I ever saw you again, I would... well, let's just say it involves my mouth and your ears.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh!

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Nyeh-HEH-nyeh!

jokes.text: I'm just saying if dogs do experience jet lag, then because of the whole seven-dog-years-to-one-human-year thing, that when a dog flies from New York to Los Angeles, he doesn't just lose three hours, he loses, like, a week and a half.
jokes.setup: Ross is on a date with Kristen and the conversation has somehow drifted to dogs and jet lag. He is working through the math in real time.
jokes.punchline: The conclusion — a dog loses a week and a half flying to LA — is reached by genuine mathematical logic that is somehow both plausible and completely ridiculous.
jokes.explanation: This is perfectly Ross — using pseudoscientific reasoning to arrive at a confident conclusion about an absurd premise. The specificity of the math ('a week and a half') and the dry delivery make this funnier than a vaguer joke would be. Only Ross monologues about dog jet lag on a first date.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'd like you to meet my date, Emily. Emily, this is Carol, my ex-wife.

dialogue.speaker: Emily
dialogue.line: Oh, so you're the woman who... I mean, Carol, it's nice to meet you.

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: Nice to meet you too.

dialogue.speaker: Emily
dialogue.line: So, um, how long were you two...?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Seven years.

dialogue.speaker: Emily
dialogue.line: Seven years. That's... that's a long time to be married to a man and then realize you're a lesbian.

jokes.text: Who are they? The, uh, blond is my ex-wife. And the woman touching her is her... close personal friend.
jokes.setup: Ross and his date see Carol and Susan across the restaurant.
jokes.punchline: 'Close personal friend' — the euphemism for 'lesbian lover' is a deliberate and comically inadequate understatement that puts off the full reveal.
jokes.explanation: The euphemism works because it delays the information while being transparently inadequate. Ross's discomfort speaking plainly about his ex-wife's relationship is character-specific and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Fireman
dialogue.line: Yeah, your boyfriend's a real bear. I mean, look at this photo—chest hair everywhere. This guy's hairier than a Sasquatch.

jokes.text: You mean they're lovers? If you want to put a label on it.
jokes.setup: Kristen pushes for clarification after Ross's 'close personal friend' euphemism.
jokes.punchline: Ross's 'if you want to put a label on it' is a commitment-avoidant non-answer that essentially confirms while refusing to confirm — the joke is his evasion.
jokes.explanation: The passive non-confirmation 'if you want to put a label on it' is a nice evasion joke — Ross can't quite bring himself to say it out loud. Character-consistent and gets a solid chuckle.

dialogue.speaker: Fireman
dialogue.line: You know, this is actually pretty common on Valentine's Day. A lot of people like to burn their ex's stuff.

jokes.text: Oh, and she's pregnant with my baby. I always forget that part.
jokes.setup: Ross has told Kristen about his ex-wife and her lesbian partner. He says 'anything else I should know?' and she says 'nope, that's it.'
jokes.punchline: Then immediately: 'Oh, and she's pregnant with my baby. I always forget that part.' The self-deprecating admission that he forgets this crucial fact is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Structurally excellent. The false resolution ('nope, that's it') followed by the immediate revelation of an enormous piece of information ('she's pregnant with my baby') is a textbook misdirection-escalation. But the real joke is the follow-up: 'I always forget that part' — Ross's casual relationship with the most un-forgettable fact of his life is absurd and perfectly in character. One of the episode's best.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: I got you a gift!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, please tell me it's a weapon.

jokes.text: All I had is oregano and a Fresca.
jokes.setup: Phoebe calls for sage branches and sacramental wine for the cleansing ritual.
jokes.punchline: Monica's substitutes — oregano (a cooking herb) and Fresca (a diet soda) — are the most Monica response possible. She has the pantry of a chef and the practicality of someone who doesn't take mysticism seriously.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of Fresca is doing enormous work here. Not 'a diet soda' or 'a ginger ale' — Fresca specifically. It's the exact soda a practical, slightly unhip person would have on hand. Excellent character integration and superb economy.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: I made you personalized candy hearts!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's... sweet. What do they say?

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Oh, things like 'Call me,' 'Where are you?' and 'Why won't you answer your phone?'

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Those aren't very romantic.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: No, but they're honest. We're not exactly lovey-dovey, are we?

jokes.text: Now we need the semen of a righteous man. Huh. Okay, Pheebs, if we had that, we wouldn't be doing the ritual in the first place.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is reciting the ingredients for the cleansing ritual.
jokes.punchline: Monica's deadpan observation that if they had access to a righteous man's semen, they wouldn't need the ritual — because that implies they'd have a righteous man — is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant. The logic is airtight: if they had a righteous man available, they wouldn't need the bad-boyfriend cleansing ritual. Monica's calm, immediate reasoning through the absurd premise is perfectly in character — she's the pragmatic one who even applies logic to witchcraft. The shock value of 'semen of a righteous man' is earned rather than cheap because the callback logic elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Janice, we need to talk. This isn't working.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Oh. My. God. You're breaking up with me again?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes, I think it's for the best.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: But I love you, Chandler! I love you so much!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Janice, no—

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Nothing you say will change how I feel about you!

jokes.text: Huh. Okay, Pheebs, if we had that, we wouldn't be doing the ritual in the first place.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has requested 'the semen of a righteous man' for the ritual.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's response is a perfect one-liner: if they had access to a righteous man, they wouldn't need to do a cleansing ritual at all.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's sharpest joke. Rachel's response is logically airtight: the whole premise of the ritual is that they can't find decent men, so requiring a righteous man's semen as an ingredient is self-defeating. The joke is clever on two levels — it's funny as a punchline AND as a structural observation. 'If we had that, we wouldn't be doing the ritual' is perfectly structured, highly quotable, and would get a genuine eruption in a comedy-savvy room. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor example in sharpness and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: We're like a ship and the sea. We're always drawn back together.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Or we're like a ship and an iceberg.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: That's not romantic!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, but it's honest. And inevitable. Ahhhhhh!

jokes.text: A picture of Scotty Jared, naked. Let me see. He's wearing a sweater. No. Ew!
jokes.setup: The women are throwing mementos into the fire. Rachel produces a photo of Scotty Jared 'naked.'
jokes.punchline: Monica requests to see it. The 'sweater' is body hair — so dense it looks like a sweater. Monica and Phoebe's overlapping reactions (denial, then disgust) are the payoff.
jokes.explanation: The body hair 'sweater' euphemism is a classic visual joke delivered through dialogue. The three-beat reaction (Monica asks, Phoebe misidentifies, Monica corrects, both react) is well-paced. 'He's wearing a sweater' as a descriptor for extreme body hair is a genuinely clever image.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I think it went pretty well. She said she'd call me.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: She left in the middle of dinner.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, but she said she'd call.

jokes.text: Wait. Isn't it almost pure...? [fire explosion implied]
jokes.setup: Rachel has produced the 'last of Paolo's grappa' to add to the fire.
jokes.punchline: Monica starts to warn that grappa is almost pure alcohol — the implication being the fire explodes. The cut or reaction tells us it went badly. The warning coming too late is the classic comedy-of-errors structure.
jokes.explanation: Interrupted warning leading to predictable catastrophe is a reliable structure. The fact that we don't see the explosion makes it slightly less impactful in transcript form, but the comedic logic is sound and the fireman scene that follows confirms it.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Maybe we should get back together.

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: Ross, I'm a lesbian.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know, but that's just a phase.

jokes.text: Oh, man. In my next life I'm coming back as a toilet brush.
jokes.setup: Chandler is contemplating having to dump Janice on Valentine's Day after already dumping her on New Year's.
jokes.punchline: The self-deprecating declaration that a toilet brush has more dignity than what he's about to do — the specific choice of 'toilet brush' (the most ignoble object possible) is the comedic detail.
jokes.explanation: 'Toilet brush' is the perfect specificity. Not 'trash' or 'dirt' but a toilet brush — the most thankless, degraded, specific object imaginable. Chandler's self-loathing expressed as a bargain-basement reincarnation wish is both funny and poignant. Strong character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, so, I've been thinking about this whole Carol situation, and I've decided to just... not acknowledge it. We can just move past it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Ross, you can't just pretend it didn't happen.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Why not? We can treat it like a meeting agenda item. Bring it up, discuss it briefly, then move on to other business.

jokes.text: Hello, funny valentine.
jokes.setup: Chandler has been dreading this moment. Janice appears at his door on Valentine's Day with candy hearts.
jokes.punchline: Janice's breezy, theatrical greeting — 'Hello, funny valentine' — is delivered with full Janice energy, oblivious to Chandler's dread. The wordplay on 'My Funny Valentine' adds a layer.
jokes.explanation: Janice at full Janice — theatrical, emotionally oblivious, with a pun on 'My Funny Valentine.' The contrast with Chandler's barely-contained panic is the comedic engine.

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: Well, I think we should see other people. You know, we're on a break.

jokes.text: Hi, just Janice.
jokes.setup: Janice has just called herself 'funny valentine.' Chandler responds.
jokes.punchline: 'Just Janice' — the deflation of her grand entrance. He refuses her theatrical framing and reduces her to the most basic identification possible. The 'just' does all the work.
jokes.explanation: Two words that perfectly capture the Chandler-Janice dynamic. He can't even give her the satisfaction of engaging with her romantic self-presentation. The deflation is maximum-economy humor — 'just Janice' is a complete comedic statement.

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: Ross, if you want to date someone, you actually have to talk to them.

jokes.text: If you don't do it, I will.
jokes.setup: Joey is being kissed all over by Janice. Chandler watches.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's threat to dump Janice himself if Joey doesn't — the 'do it' refers to breaking up with Janice, which Chandler can't bring himself to do but is apparently willing to delegate or threaten to take back.
jokes.explanation: Ambiguous at first (do what?) which adds a beat of confusion before the context clarifies. The desperation of watching Joey get kissed by your girlfriend and threatening to re-enter the situation just to end it is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Fireman
dialogue.line: So, we're inviting girls back to the firehouse. You interested?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, yes! Do you guys really ring the bell?

jokes.text: Ross's date cutting him off to take a work call mid-conversation about his teaching career
jokes.setup: Ross is earnestly explaining his career to his date. She asks what he does.
jokes.punchline: His date interrupts mid-sentence to take a work call — Ross is abandoned in the middle of his own self-introduction, left to continue talking to no one.
jokes.explanation: The cringe of being abandoned mid-sentence by your date while she takes a call, forcing you to continue talking to the air, is a relatable humiliation. Works better visually than in transcript.

dialogue.speaker: Fireman 1
dialogue.line: Yeah, we're both single, looking to settle down with the right woman.

dialogue.speaker: Fireman 2
dialogue.line: Absolutely. Honesty and trust are really important to us.

dialogue.speaker: Fireman 1
dialogue.line: We'd never cheat or lie to someone we care about.

dialogue.speaker: Fireman 2
dialogue.line: That's right. We're the kind of guys you can count on.

dialogue.speaker: Fireman 1
dialogue.line: Hey, speaking of which, I gotta get back to my other girlfriend before she realizes I'm not at the station.

dialogue.speaker: Fireman 2
dialogue.line: Oh, good call. Mine's getting suspicious about the 'extra shifts' I've been pulling.

jokes.text: So I'm spending most of my time teaching science, heh, which is funny because that wasn't even my major.
jokes.setup: Ross is continuing his introduction to his date — but she is on the phone. He continues talking as if she's listening.
jokes.punchline: The joke is that he has powered through to the second half of his career description despite clearly speaking to no one — his social obliviousness (or desperate optimism) is the character comedy.
jokes.explanation: The 'which is funny because that wasn't even my major' is Ross trying to make small talk with someone who isn't listening — his commitment to the bit (continuing regardless) is the joke. Mild but character-consistent.

jokes.text: Kristen does something... that, funnily enough... wasn't even her major.
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to introduce his date to Carol. He describes Carol's teaching job, then turns to his date's career — but he doesn't know what she does because she spent their date on the phone.
jokes.punchline: Ross uses his own earlier forgotten anecdote ('wasn't even my major') as a fill-in template for Kristen's career, because he has no actual information about her.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback structure. Ross's throwaway line about his own career becomes the only piece of information he has to describe his date — so he applies his own anecdote to her, which exposes that he learned absolutely nothing about her. The construction is tight, the callback reward is satisfying, and it's deeply character-specific to Ross's hapless first date. Strong joke.

jokes.text: Wow, that guy's hairier than the chief.
jokes.setup: Firefighters arrive to deal with the bonfire that got out of control. They are looking at the half-charred picture of Scotty Jared.
jokes.punchline: The firefighter compares the body hair in the photo to a colleague's — the specificity of 'the chief' as the benchmark for extreme hairiness is the comic detail.
jokes.explanation: Callback to the body-hair sweater joke, now confirmed and extended by an outside observer. The 'chief' benchmark is a nice world-building detail that makes the firefighters feel like real characters for a moment.

jokes.text: It's not the first boyfriend bonfire we've seen get out of control. You're our third call tonight. Valentine's is our busiest night of the year.
jokes.setup: The women are embarrassed by the fire getting out of control.
jokes.punchline: The firefighter's casual revelation that boyfriend bonfires are a regular Valentine's Day call — and that this is their third tonight — transforms a specific embarrassment into a universal phenomenon.
jokes.explanation: Great observational joke that earns its laughs through specificity: not just 'we see this a lot' but 'you're our THIRD call tonight' and 'Valentine's is our busiest night of the year.' The joke reframes Valentine's Day bitterness as a citywide phenomenon, which is both funny and darkly true.

jokes.text: I brought you something. Is it loaded?
jokes.setup: Janice arrives at Chandler's apartment for Valentine's Day. She says she brought him something.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's immediate response — 'is it loaded?' — implies he's hoping for a gun, presumably to end his romantic misery. The dark implication is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The dark implication — that Chandler is hoping for a weapon — is delivered with perfect economy and Chandler's trademark self-deprecating nihilism. The brevity makes it punch above its weight. 'Is it loaded?' is highly quotable.

jokes.text: 'Chan and Jan forever.' I had them made special.
jokes.setup: Chandler was hoping for something that might end his suffering. Janice reveals candy hearts.
jokes.punchline: Custom candy hearts reading 'Chan and Jan forever' — Janice's commitment level and the specificity of the nickname mash-up is simultaneously sweet and horrifying for Chandler.
jokes.explanation: The episode title is 'The One With The Candy Hearts' — so this is the pivotal visual joke. 'Chan and Jan forever' on personalized candy hearts shows Janice's delusion and her adorable/terrifying romanticism. The contrast with Chandler's reaction is the comedic engine.

jokes.text: Look, there's no way for me to tell you this. At least, there's no new way for me to tell you this.
jokes.setup: Chandler is trying to break up with Janice — again — on Valentine's Day.
jokes.punchline: The self-correction 'at least, there's no new way' acknowledges that he's done this before and has already exhausted the available methods. The self-awareness is dark and funny.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully crafted. The self-correction mid-sentence — from 'there's no way to tell you this' to 'there's no NEW way' — is the comedic reveal. It implies he's told her so many times he has run out of fresh approaches. This is joke writing that rewards attention. Sharp economy, perfect character integration.

jokes.text: You love me, Chandler Bing. Then why do you think we keep ending up together? New Year's, who invited who? Valentine's, who asked who into whose bed?
jokes.setup: Chandler is trying to break up with Janice. She refuses to accept it.
jokes.punchline: Janice uses the evidence of his own actions against him — he invited her at New Year's, he invited her into his bed on Valentine's — making a compelling case that he keeps choosing her, even if he denies it.
jokes.explanation: Janice's cross-examination of Chandler is funny because she's right. The humiliation of being out-argued by the person you're trying to dump is deeply character-specific — Chandler can't even break up properly.

jokes.text: Something deep in your soul calls out to me like a foghorn. Janice. Janice.
jokes.setup: Janice is making her case that Chandler loves her and can't live without her.
jokes.punchline: The 'foghorn' simile for his soul's desire — and then Chandler pathetically calling her name as if trying to interrupt a foghorn — is the absurdist image. Janice as irresistible force of nature, foghorn as her sonic equivalent.
jokes.explanation: The foghorn metaphor is inspired — it perfectly captures Janice's volume, persistence, and unavoidability. It also inadvertently positions Chandler as a ship helplessly drawn toward her. Chandler's plaintive interruptions of 'Janice. Janice.' play as a man shouting at the ocean.

jokes.text: You want me. You need me. You can't live without me. And you know it. You just don't know you know it.
jokes.setup: Janice is delivering her closing argument for why Chandler should stay with her.
jokes.punchline: 'You just don't know you know it' — the final escalating layer of denial she's assigned to Chandler. Not only is he in denial, he's in meta-denial (he doesn't know that he knows the truth).
jokes.explanation: 'You just don't know you know it' is a beautifully absurd piece of Janice logic — she's constructed a denial within a denial, making her position unfalsifiable. It's also strangely endearing because she's absolutely convinced. Strong character-specific escalation.

jokes.text: Call me.
jokes.setup: Chandler has apparently broken up with Janice. She leaves.
jokes.punchline: As a final parting shot, Janice says 'call me' — refusing to accept the breakup even as she walks away. It's a complete inversion of the expected beaten-exit.
jokes.explanation: Two words that perfectly encapsulate Janice. After a full scene of refusing to accept the breakup, she exits with 'call me' — which simultaneously acknowledges the breakup (she's leaving) and denies it (the relationship continues in her mind). Maximum economy (10.0 is justified here — it's literally two words doing the work of a paragraph). Perfect character integration. The audience response would be enormous because it both resolves and continues the joke.

jokes.text: It's not true. I never called your mother a wolverine.
jokes.setup: Ross and Carol are having a conversation. We hear only one side — Ross's denial.
jokes.punchline: The specific animal — wolverine — implies a preceding argument where Ross apparently described Carol's mother as a wolverine. The denial without context is funnier than the accusation would be.
jokes.explanation: The word 'wolverine' is doing enormous work here. It's specific, visual, aggressive, and funny. The non-sequitur nature of the denial (we don't hear the accusation, only the denial) is a good comedic structure that leaves the imagination to fill in the context.

jokes.text: Well, maybe it's cold in there.
jokes.setup: Kristen's coat is gone, implying she left. Chandler suggests she's not in the bathroom. Ross wonders if she is.
jokes.punchline: Ross refuses to accept the obvious conclusion that his date left, grasping at the explanation that her coat is still in the bathroom because 'maybe it's cold in there.'
jokes.explanation: The denial is both pathetic and endearing — Ross constructing an impossible alternative explanation rather than face the truth. 'Maybe it's cold in there' is a perfectly absurd hedge.

jokes.text: You know, this is still pretty hot.
jokes.setup: Ross has just realized his date fled. The mood is low. Chandler tries to find a silver lining.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's non-sequitur comfort — gesturing to whatever food remains — is an absurd pivot from emotional support to practical noticing. The 'still' implies this has been sitting for a while while they dealt with drama.
jokes.explanation: Quick beat of absurd positivity — finding comfort in warm food amid romantic disaster. Works as a character beat for Chandler's deflection style.

jokes.text: Mushroom. Smile. They won't all be like this. Some might even stay through dinner.
jokes.setup: Ross is devastated that his first date in years ended with the woman fleeing.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's consolation — 'some might even stay through dinner' — is a catastrophically low bar for future dating success, which is both brutally funny and weirdly comforting.
jokes.explanation: The pep talk that sets the absolute floor of expectations — 'some might even stay through dinner' — is a great piece of dark comfort. The 'even' is the crucial word; staying for dinner is being positioned as an aspiration. Chandler's empathetic nihilism at its best.

jokes.text: No, no, I know what you're gonna say. You're a lesbian. But what do you say we just put that aside for now, you know? Let's just stick a pin in it, okay?
jokes.setup: Ross is telling Carol he loves her and wants to give their relationship another shot.
jokes.punchline: 'Let's just stick a pin in it' — the suggestion that being a lesbian is a detail that can be tabled, like a scheduling conflict, is both Ross's obliviousness and his desperate romanticism distilled to a single absurd image.
jokes.explanation: Only Ross. The bureaucratic language of 'stick a pin in it' applied to his ex-wife's sexual orientation is simultaneously absurd and deeply sad. It's the kind of joke that reveals character completely — Ross's inability to process reality when his feelings are engaged. Highly quotable and genuinely original.

jokes.text: You know that thing we put over here with the pin in it? It's time to take the pin out.
jokes.setup: Ross has declared his love. Carol tells him she loves him too — but there's a 'but.'
jokes.punchline: Carol uses Ross's own 'pin in it' metaphor against him — restoring the very thing he tried to table. The callback demonstrates that Carol was listening and that the pin in his logic doesn't hold.
jokes.explanation: Elegant callback that completes the earlier joke. Ross tried to suppress the lesbian reality by metaphorically pinning it aside; Carol's calm deployment of the same metaphor to reject him is both funny and touching. The symmetry is satisfying.

jokes.text: All you need is a woman who likes men and you'll be set.
jokes.setup: Carol is consoling Ross, saying the right woman is waiting for him.
jokes.punchline: Carol's advice that Ross just needs a woman 'who likes men' — a statement that seems obvious but is a direct callback to her own sexual orientation being the problem — is darkly funny.
jokes.explanation: Carol offering the seemingly obvious tip ('find a woman who likes men') while being the reason this is relevant is a good piece of self-aware irony. The deadpan practicality of her advice is funny because she's delivering it with complete sincerity.

jokes.text: Not her. [Ross looking at woman across the room]
jokes.setup: Carol says he needs a woman who likes men. Ross looks up at the nearest available woman.
jokes.punchline: Whatever he sees makes him immediately disqualify her. The joke is in what he sees (and we might not see) — his expression and the speed of the rejection.
jokes.explanation: Quick visual beat — Ross's immediate and wordless rejection is funny in context. Works better on screen where the reaction is visible. In transcript form it's a placeholder for physical comedy.

jokes.text: We get off around midnight. Why don't we pick you up then? Great. So, um, will you bring the truck? I'll even let you ring the bell. Wohoo!
jokes.setup: The firemen who responded to the boyfriend bonfire are asking the women out.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe asking if they'll bring the truck — and her delighted 'Wohoo!' at being told she can ring the bell — treats the fire truck as a romantic perk. Her childlike enthusiasm about the bell is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's childlike excitement about ringing the fire truck bell is perfectly in character — she elevates the date by being thrilled about something the adults take for granted. The 'Wohoo!' is an earned reaction beat.

jokes.text: You tell them you're married? No way. My girlfriend doesn't know. I'm not gonna tell them.
jokes.setup: The women are celebrating their success with the firemen. Monica asks if Rachel told them she's married.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's cheerful declaration that she's hiding her relationship status — followed by Monica apparently doing the same — turns the triumphant ending into a dark button about everyone being a mess.
jokes.explanation: Dark final button — the ritual supposedly broke the bad-boyfriend cycle, but the first thing the women do is behave duplicitously. The irony closes the episode on a slightly subversive note. Works better as a structural joke than a pure laugh.

tmdb_overview: Ross's first date in nine years is on Valentine's Day with a beautiful neighbor. Susan and Carol, also out on a romantic date; end up at the same restaurant. Joey sets Chandler up on a blind date. And Phoebe, Rachel and Monica decide to spend the holiday building a boyfriend bonfire in their apartment.
insight: Valentine's Day setup yields middling returns: 49 jokes in 17 minutes, but impact stays flat.
